Welcome Back! I hope you all had a wonderful summer. Now that the Fall weather is in the air it is
time for us to head back into our shops and start turning again (if you even took a break).
Did you get a chance to work on September’s President’s Challenge? The theme was a collaborative
piece so I hope some of you got together and made some shavings. It will be interesting to see what
you have come up with.
Don’t forget to come and see Michael Blankenship’s demo Saturday, September 24th. Michael is a
blind Woodturner who has been causing quite a stir with his fascinating and entertaining demonstrations. Come and see his techniques and how he overcame what many of us would consider to be a
handicap.
Did anyone score some of the wood that has become available over the summer? Sounds like there
was interesting pieces. Anyone find a gem? Remember if you are not on the wood email list and
would like to be kept aware when trees come down and are available to us, please let Dennis know.
I was disappointed that we could not find anyone to coordinate our entry into TreeFest. It would have
been a wonderful get together and time to meet potential new members and show off what we can do.
Maybe we can try again next year.
And remember that Wednesday September 28th is our first meeting of the season. Registration will
take place so please remember to sign up and bring your dues ($45 cash or cheque payable to
GVWG). It will be nice to see everyone again and hear what they have been up to over the summer.
Happy Turning
Bill
Bill Fowle

Cover Page Image: Manitoba Maple Dish by Merv Graham (16” X 3”)
Merv is a long‐time member of the Guild and proliϔic contributor to our success. He has served on the
executive for several terms and volunteered in many other ways. He is a retired school teacher (Tech Ed)
and lives in Richmond.
Manitoba Maple (Acer negundo)has a unique red stain that is prized by woodworkers and turners alike.
It ranges from soft pink to bright red and appears whenever there is some sort of wound in the tree. The
popular belief that the staining was caused by a fungus was disproven by a 2002 study by Andrea C.
Morse and Robert A. Blanchette, Department of Plant Pathology, University of Minnesota, St. Paul. Their
paper titled Etiology of Red Stain in Boxelder was based on an 18 month controlled study of 20 trees and
concluded that the red staining was present in all trees whether the fungus was present or not.
So, we don’t know why it is like that but we are glad it is.

Focus On Fundamentals ‐ Skewing Around
Marco Berera started with a little history about
himself as a young pattern maker apprentice is
Switzerland, many many years ago.
Then Marco when on to talk a little about the skew
and the fine Finnish it can produce. He started
with a square and explained on how to make a cylinder by starting a few inches in from one end and
feed toward the end to keep the chips small and
not have splinters coming off.
He mentioned about the safe zone for good cutting
and what happens and reasons for a catch which
can happen in an instant.
He also stated that the larger the skew it is harder
to get a catch. The reason is there is a larger safe
zone.
The skews that Marco uses are manufactured tool
steels. The one exception is a file which has been
heat treated to make it safe to use. Info on heat
treating can be found on the internet. You can
start here.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heat_treating
(Continued on page 5)

I hope everyone enjoyed my June metal leafing
demonstration as much as I did preparing and presenting it. Here is a summary of the presentation.
Decorating things with gold has a long history dating back to the ancient Egyptians, Greeks, and
Chinese. For an excellent summary of the history
of gilding check out the Wikipedia pages on gilding
at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gilding
There are a number of ways of putting gold on to
various surfaces. Some require lots of special gear
while others are downright dangerous (think mercury vapour). But “leafing” is fairly simple and
safe. It involves gluing thin sheets of real or fake
(faux) metal foil to a prepared surface. There are
two main methods for doing this on wood and
which one to use can best be determined by asking
one question; “Do I want to burnish this to a high
polish?” If your answer is yes then you need to follow a quite complicated process of preparing the
surface with several coats of gesso and then using a
special glue (called sizing) that has a short working
time (around 90 minutes) where it has the right
“tack” to take the foil. But once it is applied the
gesso foundation is hard enough and the glue is
strong enough to withstand the burnishing process
traditionally done with polished agate stones called
“hounds tooth burnishers”.
If you can live without a high burnish on your piece
there is a much easier way that can be applied directly to a well sanded wood surface.
Real Vs Faux (Fake)
It is very expensive to use real gold foil. Fortunately, there are credible alternatives in copper/nickel
alloys known a faux gold (false gold). This comes
in exactly the same format as the real thing, is
about 1/60th of the cost, it is quite difficult to tell
from the real thing.
There are also a variety of other metal foils that are
readily available on-line of in better art supply
stores (Colours in Coquitalm, DeSerres in Vancouver, or Opus in Vancouver and Langley). Silver
(real and faux), aluminium, copper, and variegated
foils are all available for around $10 for a book of
25 of 5 ½” square sheets.
An additional step is required when using faux foil
as it will oxidize or tarnish unless it is sealed. Fortunately this is easy to do with a brush-on or spray
sealer.
Some artists take advantage of the oxidation and
patination with various chemicals to create wonderful results. Although it is outside the scope of
this talk I recommend looking up the work of David J. Marks
By Bruce Campbell
Metal leaϐing

Surface Preparation
It is a good idea to sand to 320 grit or better and
raise the grain several times and as the glue used in
this process is water-based.
Undercoating
If the surface is very hard (plastic, cocobolo, blackwood, lignum vitae, etc.) it may not be porous
enough to take the sizing. In this case a special undercoat called bole can be used. It is an oil-based,
sticky paint that dries to a toothy surface that takes
sizing really well. Bole is usually coloured because
the foil is so thin the colour shows through. Red is
normally used under gold and blue is under silver.
Other colours are also available.
Sizing
Once the surface is prepared it is a simple matter
of brushing or spraying on the sizing and allowing
it to “tack up” (45-60 minutes depending of temperature and humidity). The working time is up to
48 hours, again depending on temperature and
humidity.
Applying the foil
Foil comes in two main formats; loose and backed.
Loose is simply the sheet of material sandwiched
between two layers of tissue paper. The backed foil
is attached to a piece of tissue paper that easily
peels off when the foil is pressed against the sizing.
Fortunately, the tissue does not stick to the sizing.
Each piece of foil weights just a few grams and gets
blown around by the slightest draft so whenever
possible the backed version should be used – especially in a drafty room or outdoors.
But, in cases where there are tight curves or irregular surfaces like relief carving loose foil is the only
way to proceed. Sheets of foil are gently crumpled
and then dabbed on with a stiff brush where it
crumbles apart and is caught by the sticky sizing.
In some cases it can take two or three coats to get a
uniform surface.
Pressure Burnishing
The water-based sizing is not all that strong so burnishing can easily rub the foil off the surface. But,
the surface can be nicely improved by applying direct pressure and a little rubbing with a soft rag.
For an even better surface, another coat of sizing
and foil can be applied.
Sealing
(Continued on page 8)
loose leaf method
leafing a smooth hard surface

Page 8
GVWG
All metal foils other than gold need to be sealed to
prevent them from oxidizing. Gilding companies
will sell you a very clear sealer that will not discolour the foil but our trusted Wipe-On Poly works
too.
Conclusion
Water-based metal leafing is a simple, non-toxic
process that works well on wood, especially turned
pieces because of the superior smooth surfaces that
can be achieved. The wide variety of metal foils
available, the ease of application, and the control of
placement makes this an excellent method for accenting turned wood.
(Continued from page 7)

July 02 2016 was our annual Art in the Park in
Maple Ridge. Jean Ruttan & Bruce Wood handled the booth while Dan Moleschi and I did
our favorite thing; make turning tops for the
kids young and old. The crowd was delighted
and many became proud owners of tops.
Meanwhile, Keith Ruttan entertained the audience by turning bowls.
It was a hot day but thanks to Anne's tent we
were in the shade.
Thank you Dan, Jean, Bruce, Keith, and Anne
for another successful Art in the Park
(Ed Note) The Guild supports members that
demonstrate at public events by sanctioning
them as Guild events. The primary advantage of this is to extend the Guild’s liability
insurance to the activity. In return, the Guild
requires that all demonstrators are certified
by the Guild, that Guild safety standards are
followed, and that the members prominently
display Guild promotional information. To
apply in advance speak to a member of the
Guild’s Executive.
by Gerry Vickers

Beads of Courage Update
Please note that we have an excellent “Classifieds”
page on our website www.gvwg.ca where you can
list ads and find “stuff”. The page includes a “buysell-trade”, “freebies”, and a new “services/
commissioning” tab where you can list your talents for hire. Please note, that listings for the “buy
-sell-trade” will automatically be removed after 6
months, unless you otherwise tell the Webdude
(webmaster@gvwg.ca).
These listings are monitored so we don’t get a
bunch of junk on it. So to get something added
send your listings to the webmaster@gvewg.ca –
please keep them short, concise, photos are welcome, and please include a way for people to contact you.
Personally, I’ll be keeping close tabs on the freebies! I love free “stuff”
NOTE – our website is viewed around the world
so please be careful with contact information.
SPAM can be nasty (Editor)
Also, the Beads of Courage program has its own
page on our website. This is our online hub -
please check it out. There are some youngsters
out there that will benefit greatly from this worthy
cause.
On Friday Sept 9th, the Beads of Courage warehouse in Arizona packed the first batch of beads,
distribution boxes, support information and training material to BC Children’s Hospital. They are
in transit now and are expected to be here in time
for a program launch around the end of October
or mid-November.
For those who are not familiar with the program,
it is designed to take some of the pain and fear out
of the lives of sick kids dealing with chronic, acute
or life threatening ailments. Each time a child in
the program gets a treatment they get a bead coloured to correspond to that treatment. The sad
part is that some kids accumulate LOTS of beads.
And that is where we come in.
Our opportunity is to turn boxes to be given to
kids to store their beads. There are some design
restrictions including that it should be about 6” x
6”, have a durable and food-safe finish, and not
have any dangerous parts (like long thin finials).
A complete list of restrictions is available on the
Beads of Courage link on our website (http://
gvwg.ca/_BOC.html ) .
It would be great to have a Guild make a bunch of
boxes for this worthy cause. You are certainly welcome to turn boxes of your own design but if you
need some guidance Austin Texas-based turner
John Tolly worked out a neat box using 6” PVC
pipe. Club members might like to get together to
do this project en masse. I have some pipe already
and have secured a commercial price for 10 foot
sections for about $1.00 per foot so we can make
two boxes for a buck.
Please contact me directly at a meeting if you
want to be part of such a workshop
For more information, please have a look at the
Beads of Courage link on our webpage
(www.gvwg.ca/_BOC.html )
